failures.root_cause: NOT a commit regression. The assertion (a deleted user's title/fact must never resurface) is byte-for-byte identical to its original introduction at commit f4cc265 (PR #34) and fails identically AT THAT EXACT COMMIT in any environment with chromadb installed -- reproduced on macOS and inside a vanilla linux/python:3.11-slim Docker container, ruling out an OS/filesystem explanation. The real cause: NOT ONE of the 6 install commands across every job in .github/workflows/test.yml ever installed the `memory`/`docs`/`all` extras that pull in chromadb (confirmed by reading the workflow directly), so orca/brain/memory.py's LongTermMemory has silently run its JSONL-fallback code path (a plain, genuinely-clean os.unlink()) in 100% of CI runs across this project's entire ~45-PR history, never once exercising the real ChromaDB-backed deletion path. That real path's delete_collection() call removes a collection from Chroma's own query surface, but the shared chroma.sqlite3 file is one SQLite database for every session's collection -- SQLite marks a deleted row's page reusable, it does not overwrite the bytes -- so the deleted session's raw text remained physically present and recoverable on disk for as long as any OTHER session's collection kept the file from going empty (confirmed clean with only one collection ever written; confirmed NOT clean with a second, still-live collection present, which is the realistic shape of any multi-user deployment).
failures.baseline_reproduction: Historical GitHub CI for commit f4cc265 (PR #34) genuinely passed (verified via `gh api repos/.../commits/f4cc265/check-runs`) -- because that CI run, like every run since, never installed chromadb and therefore never exercised this code path.
failures.environment_dependency: Requires chromadb installed AND more than one live collection coexisting in the shared chroma.sqlite3 file. Reproducible on both macOS and Linux once that precondition holds -- not an OS-specific issue, a CI-coverage gap.
failures.security_impact: HIGH -- real, confirmed privacy defect. A deleted user's raw conversation content (facts stored via commit_to_long_term(), which runs unconditionally on every chat/stream/ultra turn, not just explicit /api/remember calls) remained forensically recoverable from disk after a complete, API-confirmed account deletion, in exactly the multi-session shape a real production deployment has. Confirmed NOT a cross-tenant LIVE-retrieval vulnerability (a colliding or otherwise unrelated session's recall() query never returns the deleted data -- verified directly), but a data-at-rest / secure-erasure gap: literal bytes remained scannable on disk.
failures.fix: orca/brain/memory.py: LongTermMemory.delete() now runs a VACUUM of the shared chroma.sqlite3 file (via a dedicated _vacuum_after_delete() method) after delete_collection() succeeds, reclaiming and overwriting the freed pages. A process-wide _CHROMA_LOCK now serializes __init__'s PersistentClient/get_or_create_collection(), store(), recall(), and delete()+vacuum against each other within one process -- the VACUUM step, run via a separate raw sqlite3 connection, was found (by this remediation's own adversarial concurrency test) to race against concurrent chromadb operations on unrelated collections, raising chromadb.errors.NotFoundError / a raw SQLite disk I/O error; the lock closes that. Disclosed, NOT fixed: the lock is process-local only and does not protect against a different OS process (a separate worker) opening the same file concurrently -- a real residual limitation under a multi-process deployment, out of scope for this pass. Disclosed, NOT fixed: VACUUM rebuilds the WHOLE shared file and briefly blocks concurrent access to every OTHER session's long-term memory on every single account deletion -- acceptable for the privacy guarantee this closes, not free; a high-traffic deployment should consider a scheduled/batched vacuum instead if this becomes a measured bottleneck. .github/workflows/test.yml: added `memory` extra to the Deterministic Unit Tests job's install line so this code path can never again go silently unexercised by CI.
failures.retest_evidence: 7 new adversarial tests added in tests/test_memory_long_term_chroma_privacy.py (deletion+raw-byte-residue, logical non-retrievability, an unrelated live session's data integrity after the triggered vacuum, restart-like reconnect, cross-tenant 8-char-prefix collision (register gap G-022), concurrent write during delete, and vacuum-failure-does-not-block-logical-deletion) -- all 7 pass; the concurrency test specifically re-run 40/40 clean after the lock fix (it failed 1/15 before the __init__ locking was added, confirming a real, now-closed race). Original test_account_deletion_removes_data_signs_the_user_out_and_does_not_resurrect_titles passes with chromadb installed. Broader regression: tests/test_memory_security.py, test_memory_store_metadata.py, test_memory_deletion_integration.py, test_product_flows_fake_ollama.py all pass (31 passed, 1 xfailed -- the known, pre-existing, unrelated G-026 streaming gap).

failures.root_cause: CONFIRMED WITH CERTAINTY, found live on real CI (not guessed): this remediation's own fix for F9 (adding the `memory` extra to the Deterministic Unit Tests job, so chromadb is actually installed) transitively imports `tokenizers` -- chromadb's default embedding function depends on it -- the first time any test in the same pytest invocation constructs a real chromadb-backed LongTermMemory/DocStore. `tokenizers` is itself one of the FORBIDDEN_TOP_LEVEL names this exact test checks for. Once imported, it stays in sys.modules for the rest of that one process regardless of execution order, so this hygiene check fails for every test file that runs in the same invocation after whichever one first imports chromadb. CI's own first real run on this remediation's commit 5e4dbafb109ea87b38037bc1502663f3e2db187f reproduced exactly this: "assert (['tokenizers', 'tokenizers.decoders', ... 14 items] == [])".
failures.baseline_reproduction: Reproduced on real GitHub Actions CI (run 38609485478, job 116008841666) on this remediation's own commit -- not a local-only or full-suite-only artifact. Confirmed NOT test-order-random: deterministic given any chromadb-touching test runs before this one in the same pytest process.
failures.environment_dependency: Any single pytest invocation that both (a) installs chromadb (this remediation's own F9 CI fix) and (b) runs this sentinel hygiene test in the same process as any chromadb-touching test. failures.root_cause: CONFIRMED, root-caused, deterministic (not a flake, not test-order interference -- initially suspected as such, then disproved by direct reproduction). orca/train/dryrun/sentinel.py's SyntheticOnlyGuard._preflight() treated 'sandbox is under the system temp dir' as SUFFICIENT for safety; it is only necessary. If the checked-out repository itself is located under the system temp directory -- exactly what happens for a disposable verification clone made under /tmp (this remediation's own earlier verification clone, /tmp/orneur-verify), a CI runner's workspace, or a Docker build context, all three of which happen in this project's own workflow -- then SyntheticOnlyGuard(REPO).__enter__() incorrectly SUCCEEDED, activating the guard's global state with nothing left to ever call __exit__() (the test's own `attempt()` helper deliberately never does, since it expects this call to raise). Every subsequent action in that same child process then tripped the now-permanently-active audit hook, including the test's own next legitimate setup step (a symlink creation), producing the exact observed traceback (SyntheticGuaranteeViolation on os.symlink).
failures.baseline_reproduction: Deterministically reproduced on demand by copying the repository to /tmp and running the exact same test from there: fails every time under that precondition, passes every time (40/40) under normal operation (repo not under tempdir). Confirmed NOT a flake: 40/40 clean solo runs before the fix, with the bug's real trigger condition identified precisely.
failures.environment_dependency: Triggers only when the checked-out repository root is itself located under the system temp directory. Reproduces identically on macOS and (implied by the mechanism being pure Python path comparison, not OS-specific) would reproduce on Linux under the same precondition.
failures.security_impact: MEDIUM -- a real integrity gap in the dry-run sentinel's own 'synthetic-only guarantee,' though NOT in the production training-authorization gate (orca/train/authorization.py), which is a separate module, unaffected and independently re-verified. If the real orca package source tree is guarded as if it were an ephemeral synthetic-only sandbox, the sentinel's core guarantee (nothing outside the sandbox is real, non-synthetic code) becomes meaningless for any process relying on it under that precondition.
failures.fix: orca/train/dryrun/sentinel.py: _preflight() now additionally rejects any sandbox whose resolved path overlaps (equals, contains, or is contained by) the real, currently-imported orca package's own source directory, independent of where that source tree happens to be checked out. A new regression test, test_fails_closed_when_the_live_orca_source_tree_is_itself_under_the_sandbox_candidate, verified failing-before (confirmed failing without the fix) and passing-after.
failures.retest_evidence: 13 tests in tests/test_trainprep_sentinel.py now pass (was 12; 1 new regression test added), confirmed 40/40 stable across repeated runs, confirmed passing both from the normal worktree location and from a /tmp-rooted copy (the exact precondition that triggered the original bug). Broader regression: the full training-authorization + trainprep suite (test_genesis_not_trained_guard.py, test_training_authorization_assurance.py, test_training_authorization_gate.py, test_trainprep_auditlog.py, test_trainprep_authorization.py, test_trainprep_binding.py, test_trainprep_budget.py, test_trainprep_checkpoint.py, test_trainprep_cli.py, test_trainprep_inventory.py, test_trainprep_ledger.py, test_trainprep_lock_env.py, test_trainprep_resume.py) -- 377 passed, 1 skipped, 1 xfailed, matching this project's own previously-recorded 377-passed baseline exactly, confirming zero collateral regression.
